title: Where New Yorkers will commemorate the anniversary of Oct. 7 and its aftermath
body: Jewish institutions in New York are gearing up to mark the third anniversary on Wednesday of Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel, as some anti-Zionist groups prepare to hold demonstrations against Israel.About 1,200 people were killed in Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel that day three years ago, most of them civilians, with another 251 taken hostage, according to Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Another 452 soldiers have been killed in the fighting since then, according to the Israel Defense Forces. In the ensuing war in Gaza, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza's Ministry of Health, which doesn't distinguish between civilians and combatants. The war has reshaped the region and reverberated around the world.Here is a list of events around New York City to commemorate the attacks and their aftermath.Manhattan's Marlene Meyerson Jewish Community Center is holding “a day of remembrance, music, and community” in its lobby, from noon until 7 p.m. “Strokes of Hope,” an exhibition of drawings by Israeli artist Zeev Engelmayer, will be on display.UJA-Federation of New York is launching “Rooted,” a public art installation at the Museum of Jewish Heritage, which will be on display until Oct. 25, made up of thousands of hostage solidarity tags and pins. At 92NY on the Upper East Side, Claire Shipman – the former acting president of Columbia University – is moderating a conversation between an Israeli father, Jonathan Dekel-Chen, and a Palestinian father, Jaser AbuMoussa.Omer Shem Tov, an Israeli former hostage, will speak at Yeshiva University's memorial at 8 p.m. In Brooklyn, the Park Slope Jewish Center will host an event at 7 p.m. including personal testimony from Atir Vinnikov, a survivor of the Nova music festival massacre.At 7 p.m. in Union Square, the group Israelis for Peace is set to meet for an evening of “quiet reflection and mourning” of the people killed on Oct. 7 and in “its bloody aftermath.”Anti-Zionist student groups planning walkoutsA number of anti-Zionist student groups are planning walkouts on campuses across the city, including City University of New York campuses, Columbia and NYU.The walkouts will culminate in a rally held outside City Hall at 4 p.m., organized by Pal-Awda and endorsed by a number of groups, calling on Mayor Zohran Mamdani, himself a strident critic of Israel, to stop “[capitulating] to Zionist pressure.”

title: IDF, Police, Shin Bet hold joint assessment in preparation for upcoming 'sensitive' election season
body: An assessment held by the IDF, Israel Police, and the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) was held to prepare for the upcoming weeks' “sensitive period,” the organizations announced in a joint statement on Wednesday.The meeting aimed to ensure “proper and safe conduct” for the upcoming elections, the statement said.Chief of Staff Major General Aial Zamir, Police Commissioner Major General Danny Levy, and Shin Bet Director David Zini attended the meeting and agreed on a series of measures to leverage the advantages of each organization.During the meeting, security officials reviewed the intelligence situation on all of Israel's borders, as well as within the country. Additionally, efforts to improve and strengthen multi-agency defense, combat terrorist organizations, and address the phenomenon of nationalist crime were also discussed. The meeting occurred as the IDF released a summary of defense accomplishments on the third anniversary of the October 7 Massacre. This is a developing story.

title: Three years later, October 7 is still not in the past for Israelis - editorial
body: Three years ago this morning, Israel woke up to the unimaginable.Hamas terrorists had breached the Gaza border, overrun communities and army bases, attacked a music festival, murdered some 1,200 people, and dragged 251 hostages into Gaza – all within hours, as the country suffered its deadliest day since its founding.Three years later, it can be tempting to think of October 7 as a dark moment that belongs to the past. But Israel has never really had the chance to put it there.The war that began that morning has yet to be fully resolved. Hamas has not been fully disarmed, its future in Gaza remains unsettled, and the questions of who will govern Gaza and what will prevent another October 7 remain unanswered.Beyond Gaza, Iran and its proxies remain a threat, and Israel continues to confront a region in which the possibility of another war is never far away.Life after October 7 is more about learning to live with what happenedFor much of the country, then, the past three years have been less about moving on from October 7 than about living with its consequences – and with the questions it left behind.But for many Israelis, October 7 is not simply something they have been living with. They are still living it.For former hostages, freedom itself remains a daily reminder of what was taken from them. Emily Damari, abducted and wounded from her home in Kfar Aza, has spoken about how captivity changed her relationship with the most ordinary parts of life.“Today, I open the fridge, and I say thank you,” Damari said. “I drink cold water, and I say thank you.”Eli Sharabi spent 491 days in captivity after being taken from Kibbutz Be'eri. His wife, Lianne, and their daughters, Noiya and Yahel, were murdered on October 7. His brother Yossi was taken hostage and died in Gaza. After his release, Sharabi said he had learned in captivity “how precious every moment and every choice can be.”“I choose life,” he said. “I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do.”For Hagar Brodutch, who was abducted with her three children and a neighbor's daughter, returning to life has been a more complicated process than the word “freedom” might suggest. She has described the immense daily struggle, particularly for children, and recently began taking pastry-baking classes as a way to build something new.“This is about much more than learning how to bake,” she said. “It is about finding a new path, creating something with my own hands, and slowly building a future.”Then there are those for whom there can be no return to the life they had before October 7.Michal Negri's son, Maj. (res.) Roee Negri, 28, was killed fighting Hamas terrorists in Kibbutz Be'eri after spending the day rescuing civilians.How can Israelis hold their government accountable after October 7?In an interview with The Jerusalem Post, Negri said that three years had done little to diminish the questions raised that morning. Above all, she wants those responsible for the failures leading up to October 7 to be held accountable through a state commission of inquiry.“Everyone that was in the government, in any position of management, has to take responsibility and be inquired into, so we will be sure that it will never happen again,” she said.“How can you be sure that it will not happen again if you don't inquire and ask questions?”That question is larger than one bereaved mother.Israel has changed dramatically since October 7, with the country's political and defense establishments learning painful lessons about its enemies, its defenses and its own institutions. But lessons must be implemented, failures examined, decisions questioned – and responsibility determined.Three years later, Israel still has no state commission of inquiry into the worst national disaster in its history.That means October 7 remains unfinished business. For many Israelis, October 7 is not three years ago – it is both the past and the present.Ahead of Israel's national elections, Israelis must remember that our enemies aren't within, but those seeking to destroy us. May the memory of those killed on October 7, 2023, and since, be blessed.

title: Three years later, I still think about the stories we did not tell on October 7- comment
body: There are families who wrote to me after October 7 and never received an answer. Others heard back too late. They sent photographs, names, and stories of people they loved, hoping we would write about them in The Jerusalem Post. Some of those stories never appeared.To those families, I am sorry.I understood what they were asking. After a terrorist attack, part of our job is to call the families and write about the people who were killed. An article can stay with a family for years. Somebody searches a name and finds something about the person: what they did, who loved them, what their friends remember.After October 7, the numbers kept going up. Hundreds, then more than a thousand. We did not even know who had been killed, who was missing, and who had been kidnapped. Meanwhile, we were covering a war and trying to explain to readers abroad what had happened.I remember looking through casualty lists and wanting an article about each person. Families were sending messages, press releases were arriving, and we used what we could get to. Sometimes a relative reached a reporter who had time to make the calls. Sometimes a message was buried under hundreds of others.More accounts of heroism, faith, and horror than we could handleI don't know how many more reporters we would have needed just to write those stories. We had more than we could handle, every day. That still bothers me, especially when I think about how much harder it may be to find those families' stories years from now.Take Tamar and Yonatan Kedem-Siman Tov and their children Arbel, Shahar and Omer, who were murdered in Nir Oz. Yonatan's mother, Carol, was murdered there too. The kibbutz's memorial page recalls that Yonatan, known as Johnny, made sure the field was watered before its kite festival to keep the dust down. I wish we had published more of those details about more people.When we looked through testimonies for our October 7 cover, there were accounts of heroism, faith, and Hamas's antisemitism. Others described Arab and Jewish Israelis helping each other. There were so many powerful stories. Naama's hit us in the stomach. She was 17, from Kfar Aza, and she thought she was going to die. On her grandfather's prescription, she wrote:“Naama of a few hours from now, if you are reading this, you are alive.” 0710JDN01She couldn't find a pen, so she used eyeliner. We kept coming back to that: her grandfather's prescription, whatever she had available to write with, and the thought that she might survive to read it. At 17, she had left a message for herself on the small chance that she would get through those hours.It was also very visual. A prescription is familiar to readers almost anywhere. They can imagine that piece of paper in their own home, belonging to a parent or grandparent. These ordinary details helped explain what we wanted the cover to convey about the everyday people caught in the attack.Testimonies, hope for a futureThere was hope in her sentence, too. She allowed for a future, even one only a few hours away, and lived to describe what she had written. The illustration on our cover is based on that account, recorded by Edut 710.We chose one testimony for the cover knowing how many others deserved that space. I hope readers who look up Naama's account will stay with the archive and listen to someone else as well.Edut 710 began as a volunteer initiative after the attack. Witnesses can tell their accounts at their own pace, including life before October 7 and what followed. Their consent governs publication and use. A detail that a reporter might have left out to meet a deadline can remain available to someone studying the account decades later.Its Smart Archive, developed with the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, makes the testimonies searchable in Hebrew and English. That gives readers overseas a way to find accounts that never reached an international newspaper.Organizations doing this work need money to continue. Volunteers need equipment, recordings need editing and translation, and somebody has to look after the material for years. Those considering a donation should think about supporting that work beyond the anniversary, when it will still need doing.We know from the Holocaust how much depends on what is collected while witnesses are still able to speak. Letters, photographs and recorded accounts allow people born decades later to examine what happened. October 7 is already being denied and distorted. The material we preserve has to be accurate, properly attributed and available for others to examine, with uncertainty acknowledged and errors corrected.Families have a part in this as well. A relative may be the only person who can identify someone in a photograph or explain why an object mattered. That knowledge can be recorded now, with their consent, rather than left for somebody to guess at later.Our cover gives space to a teenager who wrote something she thought she might never read. Because her account was recorded, readers can hear her tell it herself. There are many more people we should be listening to.I keep thinking about the families who wanted us to know who their loved ones had been. I want us to keep making room for those stories in the Post, and to help readers find the accounts being collected elsewhere.We could not tell every story then. We still have a responsibility to try now.

title: The Oct. 7 battle for Sderot still rages in the minds of its survivors
body: Shalom Aida was at home when the first air raid siren sounded at 6:29 a.m. on October 7, 2023, but he wasn't initially fazed.Rocket sirens were a common occurrence in his city of Sderot, which is less than a mile from Gaza at its closest point.   It wasn't until he heard gunshots that Aida, a retired police officer, realized that dozens of heavily armed Hamas terrorists had infiltrated Sderot and were gunning down any civilian, soldier, or police officer they came across. By the time he arrived at the police station, “it was a battlefield,” he said. The sight almost paralyzed him. “The entire street in front of the station was full of bloodied people. Police, civilians, dead or dying. Hamas kept firing.”    One of the police officers killed that day was Aida's cousin. Many others were his friends.  Three years later, he is still haunted by the memories. “Sderot seems quiet now, but it's not quiet or peaceful inside our heads,” he said as he watched groups of visitors walk around the Sderot Memorial and Heroes Park. It sits on the site of the police station, which was destroyed that day and rebuilt elsewhere. Wouldn't dream of moving elsewhere, Aida saysDespite the ongoing trauma of Oct. 7 and its aftermath, Aida said he wouldn't dream of moving elsewhere. “I never once thought about leaving,” he said, shocked by the question. “The best people in the world live in Sderot.” Not all residents of the “Gaza Envelope” who experienced the horrors of Oct. 7 returned home when the government gave the all-clear, after ordering them to evacuate for their own safety. But the vast majority of Sderot's residents —  set at over 37,000 by the Central Bureau of Statistics in 2024 —  who had already lived through two decades of rocket barrages from Gaza, returned to the city within months.   Once it was a struggling development town where successive governments sent immigrants who had just arrived from the Middle East and the former Soviet Union. It generated domestic and international headlines over the last two decades, as it became the first city hit by Hamas rockets as early as 2001, and remained one of the places the Gaza-based terror group has most frequently targeted.  International dignitaries, including UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon in 2009 and then Sen. Barack Obama during his 2008 presidential campaign, visited Sderot.   Initially a city without adequate protective shelter for its residents, it became the only place in Israel where every single apartment and bus stop has its own bomb shelter. City has prospered despite challengesDespite it all, the city has prospered: gleaming new apartment buildings, parks and a sprawling mall greet visitors as they enter. “If you were to input all the data about Sderot into OpenAI, the 25 years of rockets and Oct. 7 and the bomb shelters, it would say this must be a ghost town. But that's not the reality here,” said Ilan Abecassis, a retired educator and now tour guide who has lived in the city all his life. Rather than shrinking, he said, the city's population has grown by about 5,000 people since the Oct. 7 attack. “I know it's counterintuitive, but the more they try to destroy us, the stronger we become,” Abecassis said. “In the Torah, a new pharaoh sees the Israelite population growing and enslaves them. But the Torah tells us 'the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew.' We are like those Israelites.” Arie Yagudaev, 30, from Sderot, and his cousin Eitan Izayev, 28, who lives in nearby Kibbutz Nir Am, said they are also committed to staying, even after they encountered terrorists in the street on Oct. 7. Drinking strong coffee outside his family's grocery store in Sderot, Izayev recounted how he had begged his cousin to pick him up from the kibbutz, which terrorists were trying to infiltrate, so he could help defend loved ones in Sderot. Along the way, they picked up two teenage girls, survivors of the Nova music festival.“As we approached the roundabout into Sderot, we saw some pickup trucks ahead of us,” Izayev recalled. “We thought the men in the bed of the truck were IDF soldiers. But when the terrorists saw us, they shot at us nonstop.”  “One of the bullets shattered my car's back window. It's a miracle we survived,” Yagudaev said. Even though he suffered from PTSD every night as an evacuee in an Eilat hotel room, he said, “I wanted to go home.”   “It wasn't just because the hotel room was cramped,” he said. “Leaving Sderot and Israel is exactly what the terrorists want. We're not going anywhere.”One Sderot restaurant owner, who was born and raised in Sderot but moved to Kibbutz Nir Am several years ago, feels the same way.  “Not to return would be rewarding Hamas for its terrorism,” said the restaurant owner who requested anonymity because of his ongoing stints in the IDF reserves.    As it was, he and his wife and baby spent almost a year in a small Tel Aviv hotel room before returning to their kibbutz two years ago. It wasn't an easy homecoming, he said. For one thing, IDF soldiers had lived in their empty house, and it needed major repairs. Returning to the area also triggered traumatic memories from the Hamas attack. “For 22 hours I stood outside our house to protect my wife and newborn baby,” he recalled, sitting at a table in his restaurant. “Eventually we decided to flee in our car with just the clothes we could throw into a trash bag. We placed the baby under the seat of the car, hoping to protect him.” Once the owner of three restaurants, he now owns only one. He needed to sell the two popular restaurants he owned at another kibbutz because he couldn't operate them from Tel Aviv, and, back then, the Gaza border was an active war zone. Although the Gaza border is much more secure due to the buffer zone the IDF maintains in Gaza, “it's not quiet on the border,” he said. “We live one kilometer from Gaza. Every day we hear the choppers and the shooting.”Still, he and his wife have no plans to leave. “My parents live here, my grandparents live here,” he said. “On Oct. 7 I saw an apocalypse, bodies on the ground. I knew 100 people who were killed or kidnapped. The ground beneath us is soaked with their blood. I can't leave.”

title: Philadelphia teacher passing as Palestinian raised alarms for Jewish groups before she rose to fame
body: The first time most of the world heard Hannah Gann's name was in late September, when the 34-year-old Philadelphia high school teacher and activist confessed to having fabricated a Palestinian and Black identity — with media reports revealing she was Jewish in real life. But Jason Holtzman, director of Philadelphia's Jewish Community Relations Council, first heard Gann's name long before that: in December 2023.At that time, he recalled to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, she “made some pretty strident remarks” at a local rally called “Flood Philly For Palestine,” an apparent reference to the “Al-Aqsa Flood,” Hamas's name for its Oct. 7, 2023, attacks.In a video from the event shared with JTA, Gann said in reference to children in Gaza, “We owe them to take it to the streets and f–k the police until Palestine is free.”Gann would appear on the JCRC's radar several more times before her name hit the news for being “the Palestinian Rachel Dolezal,” when her story — accompanied by Philadelphia Inquirer reporting that she has Jewish family living in Israel — ricocheted across the internet to gain her instant notoriety. (The real-life Dolezal, a white woman who posed as Black for years and held a NAACP leadership role while teaching Africana Education at a Pacific Northwest college, has meanwhile expressed interest in meeting Gann.)Gann's revelations have led to the dissolution of the local pro-Palestinian educators group she had helped to lead since 2024. After leaving her Instagram confessions public for more than a week, Gann's account was deactivated in the last few days.Yet now that Gann's background has grabbed headlines, Jewish groups alarmed by her behavior said the real story is being missed.  “It's just being reported as if she simply is guilty of fraud, that she's the new Rachel Dolezal,” Holtzman told JTA. “It's missing part of the story, which is that she's also an extremist who has spread antisemitic tropes and has brought inflammatory content into the classroom.”A general view of the School District of Philadelphia offices on December 31, 2015 in Philadelphia City. (Paul Marotta/Getty Images)A catalog of troubling incidentsIn the JCRC's monitoring of the School District of Philadelphia, Gann's name pops up often. In 2024 she helped organize a pro-Palestinian “teach-in” project, an unofficial event staged for teachers in the district that the JCRC says “directed educators to materials that erased Israel from maps” and “characterized October 7 as 'resistance.'” That year she also posted an Instagram image of a fist rising from the ground holding a firearm, with paragliders — a symbol of the Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023 — visible in the background, one of many social media posts of hers that employed extreme language or imagery around Israel. A key part of Jewish critics' charges, that Gann brought her activism into the classroom or into her lesson plans, is harder to pinpoint. But in one screenshot of her whiteboard that she posted to social media, Gann appeared to have planned a lesson on “Black Power & Palestine.” In addition, district personnel who had visited her class in 2024 found that it “contained a 'Palestine will be free' poster, a Palestinian flag, a keffiyeh, and a map of Israel filled with a keffiyeh design,” Holtzman claimed. Gann did not respond to multiple JTA requests for comment. JCRC officials and a local Jewish activist group had pushed the district to discipline Gann over her conduct before the scandal over her identity broke — including, they said, presenting the superintendent with a full record of Jewish parent concerns this March. But such efforts, they say, fell largely on deaf ears. “We've pointed this out to the school district many times over the years,” Holtzman told JTA. He added that, in the JCRC's view, Gann's rally appearances and social media activity were in violation of district codes of conduct governing staff activity that could damage the district's reputation — with her recent admission of falsifying her ethnic identity potentially violating an ethics code requiring employees to avoid falsification in their personal records.“And they've basically done nothing about it,” he said.It wasn't only Holtzman and the JCRC urging the School District of Philadelphia to take some kind of action against Gann. Local Jewish activists filed a federal civil rights complaint against her and fellow activists in the district with whom she had formed a coalition, even entering into mediation with the district in an effort to establish new guidelines around personnel behavior. The complaint argued, among other points, that Gann's social media — where she has posted many controversial messages about Israel — should be considered an extension of her classroom.Yet Gann continued to teach 10th grade at The Workshop School, a public high school in West Philadelphia with a focus on project-based learning. Under pressure from her fellow activists, she recently came clean about her identity. A surprising confession“I lied about my family and have been lying for years,” she wrote on Instagram on Yom Kippur. “I have no Palestinian or Tunisian heritage. I am a white woman of significant privilege and wealth. Anyone who supported me was manipulated.”Gann's confession took even the Philadelphia Jewish groups who had been tracking her behavior by surprise. They told JTA they had not realized she had been identifying herself as Palestinian, nor that she was actually Jewish. Some of her fellow activists, in their own social media posts, said she had confided to them in the past that she was Jewish — while also continuing to insist she was Palestinian. While the Philadelphia Inquirer has quoted activists accusing her of having “Israeli settler family,” it was unclear to the Jews who spoke to JTA whether Gann's Israeli family actually lived in settlements in the occupied West Bank or whether the activists simply refer to all Israelis as settlers. Giving public comment at prior school board meetings, Gann had proclaimed, “I can't visit my family in Palestine,” and “I have pushed myself to teach through the agony of my family living in a warzone, and only taken one day off this entire school year.”To some Jews, such parsing is almost beside the point; they see the entire conversation around Gann's identity as a distraction. The bigger story, they said, is that she was using her position as a public school educator to push anti-Israel advocacy that included falsehoods about Israel without fear of punishment: a microcosm of what they see as a larger trend of growing pro-Palestinian sentiment among K-12 educators in many school districts and teachers' unions that has raised alarm among Jewish groups.A spokesperson for an ad hoc group of Jewish educators and families in the Philadelphia area, who asked to remain anonymous owing to what they viewed as death threats from a member of Gann's former coalition, told JTA in a statement that the district failed to express interest in Gann until the scandal.“Harm to the Jewish community is never addressed or rectified” by the district, the representative for the School District of Philadelphia Jewish Family Association (SDP JFA) said in an email.A spokesperson for the School District of Philadelphia declined to comment on whether the district would be disciplining Gann or if it had communicated with Jewish groups about her behavior prior to last week.“The District is making support available to the Workshop School staff and students, as needed,” the spokesperson wrote in an email to JTA.Meanwhile, one of the pro-Palestinian activist groups formerly associated with Gann, Philly Educators for Palestine, announced last week that “after much reflection,” it would dissolve, though “The work continues.” Its parent group, the Racial Justice Organizing Committee, said it would be going on hiatus.Prior to its announcement, Philly Educators for Palestine had publicly disassociated from Gann and had called for the district to discipline her. “It's one of the first times where I think that I really have common ground with the Philadelphia Educators for Palestine,” Holtzman quipped. Pro-Palestinian demonstrators block roads as they rally in front of Philadelphia City Hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on September 10, 2024, ahead of the presidential debate between US Vice President and Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris and Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump. (Andrew Thomas / AFP via Getty Images)Civil rights complaint filedIn 2024, SDP JFA filed a Title VI civil rights investigation with the U.S. Department of Education against a group of pro-Palestinian teachers in the district, alleging, among other things, that students had been targeted on the basis of their Jewish identity. Joining the complaint were the JCRC, the Anti-Defamation League and StandWithUs, a pro-Israel advocacy group. The groups eventually proceeded to mediation with the district, which agreed to institute changes such as drafting a district-wide anti-harassment statement; undergoing an anti-discrimination policy review; and instituting new training for staff, according to a copy of the resolution agreement viewed by JTA. Jewish groups, however, charge that the recommendations were never fully implemented.The names of the teachers in the federal investigation were redacted in official filings. But according to emails shared with JTA, Gann was one of the named parties in the ADL's amended complaint. “Evidence suggests that Ms. Gann is utilizing her actual classroom and social media platforms as a digital extension of her classroom to disseminate antisemitic rhetoric, engage in prohibited political campaigning, and promote extremist ideologies to her students,” a letter sent by SDP JFA this May reads. Following that email, Gann on Instagram made oblique references to the allegations, calling her unnamed critics “genocide enthusiasts who love to call the School District about what I'm teaching.” She also posted a fake lesson plan from her classroom whiteboard with scheduled “lessons” including “Jesus Was Palestinian.”The Jewish parents and teachers in SDP JFA say their frustrations with Gann are also informed by an even more antagonistic encounter with Keziah Ridgeway, a fellow teacher and former ally of Gann's who at one point had joined Gann in holding signs reading “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” at a school board meeting. In 2024, following a controversy around one of Ridgeway's lesson plans and an SDP JFA campaign against her, Ridgeway, believing herself targeted by Jewish online harassers, posted several of the group members' names to Instagram. In posts viewed by JTA, she accompanied this list with another post referencing the phrase, “Ain't no fun when the rabbit got the gun,” which refers to a sudden reversal in power dynamics. In a third post, Ridgeway asked followers for recommendations for “Black owned [gun emoji] shops in or near Philly.” The Jewish parents interpreted the series of posts as a threat directed at them, and reported Ridgeway to the district, ultimately leading to her suspension for a year; she has sued the district, alleging anti-Islamic bias. Gann forcefully advocated for Ridgeway's reinstatement at board meetings. Following Gann's recent revelations, Ridgeway, too, disowned her in an Instagram video. “I can no longer be in community with someone who caused so much harm,” Ridgeway wrote on social media.Ridgeway declined to comment to JTA, citing ongoing litigation.Even if they feel it's for the wrong reasons, the members of SDP JFA still want to see action taken against Gann. They are seeking to capitalize on her newfound infamy by renewing their calls to district officials to discipline her and “ameliorate the damage done to the Jewish community.” Such demands echo communications Jewish parents have sent to the district for the better part of two years. In an email to administrators last year, they sought to sum up their complaints: “Allowing Ms. Gann to remain in a teaching position sends the message that Jewish students' safety and dignity are not valued — that their teacher can publicly call for their eradication without consequence.”

title: 'Captivity comes back to you': Gilboa-Dalal reveals psychological toll three years after Oct 7
body: Content warning: This article discusses sensitive topics such as sexual assault. Former Gaza hostage Guy Gilboa-Dalal revealed the psychological toll from the sexual abuse he suffered during more than two years in Hamas captivity in an interview for Taboo on Kan 11 three years after the October 7 Massacre.Gilboa-Dalal was certain his life would be "perfect" the moment he returned home. "You think to yourself, when you're in captivity, 'I'll come back, and it will basically be perfect.' But when you are there, you aren't aware of the rehabilitation process that you have to go through when you return," he reflected. "You get home, you go to sleep, and the captivity comes back to you. There are actual nightmares of the kind that hurt me, and I run for my life," Gilboa-Dalal shared.'Is this my fault? Did I do something wrong?'He described the night terrors that plague him as a result of the trauma and sexual assault he endured at the hands of one of his captors: "I have many nightmares about the guy who sexually assaulted me. When I was there, I had so, so many thoughts running through my head of... 'Is this my fault? Did I do something wrong?', and I know that many people who go through this, those thoughts cross their minds too. And many choose not to talk about it."Later, he recounted the threats he received from that same sexual assailant, who tried to silence him: "It is very, very hard, and for me it was even harder because we had a camera on us 24/7. Because of that, I couldn't even tell my friends there about what I went through, about the sexual assault, because that guy told me he would hear everything, and I was terrified to talk about it.""I did find a way to tell Tal, in very broad strokes, about what happened, because I knew he was going home, and it was important to me that if I didn't come back alive, he would tell my family," he shared.Gilboa-Dalal was abducted from the Nova festival on October 7, 2023, and was held captive by Hamas in the Gaza Strip for over two years. Throughout the captivity period, he was moved between various positions in tunnels underneath Gaza, held under harsh conditions, and suffered from starvation, threats, and abuse. He returned to Israel in October 2025, after 738 days in Hamas captivity.

title: Former hostage Gadi Moses accuses Netanyahu of resisting Oct. 7 inquiry for political purposes
body: Former Hamas hostage Gadi Moses accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of opposing a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 massacre because of political consequences, in an interview with Kan News on Monday."I think the prime minister knows exactly what happened, and he is simply opposed to a state commission of inquiry," Moses said.Moses, 82, was kidnapped from his home in Kibbutz Nir Oz on October 7 and released after 482 days in Hamas captivity. His partner, Efrat Katz, was killed during the massacre.His comments came as the establishment of a state commission of inquiry has remained a hot political issue ahead of Israel's election on October 27. Nearly three years after the massacre, no state commission has been created, while members of the opposition have pledged to create one if they form the next government.'We must talk about tomorrow' Moses plans for future Moses said Netanyahu's leadership also contributed to divisions within Israeli society."Netanyahu 'won' to create such a difficult separation between the different tribes of the people of Israel and caused the loss of trust in the 'togetherness,'" he said.When asked about Israel's future alongside Palestinians, Moses said, “I don't think we can talk about peace today, but we must talk about what will happen tomorrow. The Palestinians are not going anywhere, and we are not going anywhere.“'There is no one to make peace with' is an empty slogan. They will understand that they have the right to exist, and they will also understand that we are here forever and no one will drive us out of here.”Security situation at Gaza border insufficient, residents living in fear, Moses saysHe also criticized the security situation around Nir Oz, saying residents continued to live in fear despite the military presence near the Gaza border.Moses returned to Nir Oz after 482 days in captivity and has since become a leading voice for rehabilitation efforts for his kibbutz following the devastation of October 7."The state does not provide us with any security that something like this cannot happen again," he added.The former hostage also called for a change in the way Israelis discuss the trauma caused by the October 7 attack."The wound is open; there are people suffering existential wounds," Moses said. "We need to change the way we speak to each other, speak more gently and relate to the difficulties of people who have experienced trauma.""'Together we will win' means together we will be one people, not together we will beat each other," he said.

title: Trump, Putin to discuss suspected plague case as US officials press Russia for answers
body: US President Donald Trump said that US intelligence agencies were in "deep discussions" over the suspected case of pneumonic plague in Russia while talking to reporters on Tuesday. He also said he would be speaking with Russian President Vladimir Putin "very soon," and promised that he would be able to report more on the case soon, "probably tomorrow."Russia has not shared an official cause of the death of 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who worked as a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. Russia's official public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, stated that Shipilova died on Friday of "pneumonia of unknown etiology."However, early local reports and statements from local officials said that Shipilova had died of the pneumonic plague. Rubio warns against speculation, says US operating with limited informationUS Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that the US was operating with limited information. "Maybe there's nothing there, maybe it's bigger than we thought, we don't know," he said. "It would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate about what this might or might not be or what this is or what this isn't," he added.Rubio also called upon Russia to share additional details. "It's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," he said. The US has also warned Russia that it may be violating its international health obligations by failing to disclose additional details of the case, the Wall Street Journal cited US officials as saying on Tuesday. A State Department spokesperson told WSJ that the department has requested additional information from the Russian government and is in official communication with other countries to share information, according to the report. Russia is a part of a 2005 global health pact called the International Health Regulations, which requires countries to notify the World Health Organization (WHO) of an event that could become an international public health emergency. Countries that identify such an event are required to provide the WHO with detailed updates on tests, lab results, and anti-epidemic measures. Rospotrebnadzor stated that no microorganisms linked to Shipilova's work were found during analyses of her body and that of almost 200 individuals tested; the only infections they found were two cases of COVID-19 and two of rhinovirus. However, Moscow has not shared which tests were conducted, according to the WSJ's report.

title: Houthis launch missiles at Yemen's Aden airport as fighting intensifies
body: Two missiles launched by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis targeted the international airport of Yemen's southern port city of Aden early on Wednesday, but no casualties were reported, the media office of Aden's security department said.The attack comes amid renewed fighting after weeks of Houthi advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast and a Saudi-backed government counteroffensive that has recaptured areas around the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait with coalition air support.The airport is the main international gateway serving parts of Yemen outside Houthi control.Saudi coalition intercepts missiles aimed at Riyadh, Khamis MushaitLater on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis north of the Saudi capital of Riyadh.Earlier, the coalition had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported.The coalition said the missile threats had originated from the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa and the governorates of Saada and Amran.Following the coalition's statement, Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV said Saudi forces carried out a strike in an area spanning the central governorates of Ibb and Taiz. There was no immediate confirmation from the Saudi-led coalition.

title: Trump orders firing squad for gunman who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas
body: US President Donald Trump has ordered the use of a firing squad to execute the former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree the gunman later described as retaliation for US wars in the Muslim world, the Pentagon said.Putting former US Army Major Nidal Hasan to death by Army firing squad was approved by Trump at the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X/Twitter on Monday.Parnell noted that Hasan shouted "Allahu Akbar" — God is greatest in Arabic — during the attack, which killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others.Acting US Army Secretary Adam Telle said on X on Tuesday that the execution by firing squad will take place on December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas.Death by firing squad was one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation.The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also proved challenging to carry out for other reasons at times.Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched an attempt to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalized.Her lawyers said on Tuesday she regained consciousness. "Her prognosis remains unclear, but at a minimum we expect a long recovery," the lawyers said on Tuesday.Pike's lawyers had previously urged the Tennessee Department of Correction to consider an alternative to lethal injection, such as hanging or firing squad, in anticipation of the trouble executioners faced in establishing a sound intravenous line.Hasan found guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder, attempted premeditated murderA military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military base.The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair after being shot by police during his arrest.In a statement responding to Trump's decision, the group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said: "There is nothing Donald Trump loves more than the power to kill."Military executions are rare, and under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, a death sentence imposed by court-martial may not be carried out "until approved by the president."If Hasan is put to death, it would mark the first military execution since 1961, the group said. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The apparent last known execution by a US military firing squad was one carried out "by musketry" in November 1945, the center reported.At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

title: US attacks damaged 111 petrochemical, medical sites in Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 07 (MNA) – Iran's representative in The Hague said the US military aggression against Iran's chemical industry damaged 111 petrochemical and pharmaceutical facilities and affected supply chains.
Iran's mission in The Hague published portions of remarks by Hadi Farajvand at the 113th session of the Executive Council of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, announcing that during US attacks, 60 petrochemical complexes, 44 pharmaceutical factories and seven pharmaceutical facilities in Iran were damaged.
Farajvand, referring to the consequences of these attacks, said the damage inflicted on Iran's chemical and pharmaceutical industries has disrupted supply chains and affected the process of implementing obligations related to the Chemical Weapons Convention.
Iran's permanent representative to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons also stressed that protecting chemical facilities against armed conflict is essential for preserving the integrity of the convention, peaceful activities in the chemical field and international cooperation.
He added that deliberate US attacks on these facilities have raised serious concerns regarding Articles 1, 6 and 11 of the Chemical Weapons Convention, as well as the goals and purposes of this international document.
According to the text of the convention, Article 1 is devoted to the general obligations of member states regarding the prohibition of chemical weapons, Article 6 covers non-prohibited chemical activities, and Article 11 emphasises international cooperation and economic and technological development in the field of peaceful chemical activities.
In another part of his remarks, Farajvand once again raised Iran's concerns about US compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention, saying these concerns relate to Washington's role in the Israeli regime's chemical weapons programme and the US programme in the field of non-lethal and incapacitating chemical weapons.
He stressed that more than two decades on, the concerns raised in this regard remain unanswered and unresolved.

title: More than 220,000 Ukrainians left country in first half of 2026
body:
MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. About 223,000 Ukrainians left the country between January and June 2026, according to data from Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service obtained by TASS.
A total of about 7.130 million departures from Ukraine and about 6.907 million entries into the country were recorded in the first half of 2026.
The outflow of people from Ukraine has continued for several years, although the border remains closed to a significant portion of the population - men of conscription age. About 7-8 million people left the country in 2022, around 180,000 in 2023, 460,000 in 2024 and 302,000 in 2025. The exact number of residents remaining in Kiev-controlled territory is unknown as the last population census was conducted in 2001. Various estimates put the figure at between 20 million and 30 million people.

title: Kim Jong Un Calls Russia’s War in Ukraine ‘Sacred’ in Putin Birthday Message
body:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un pledged his “invariable support” for Russia and praised Moscow’s war against Ukraine as a “sacred war of justice” in a birthday message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, underscoring the deepening military alliance between Pyongyang and the Kremlin.
The message was published Wednesday, Oct. 7 – Putin’s 74th birthday – by North Korea’s state-run Korean Central News Agency.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I am pleased to have good friendship with you and open up a new chapter for the development of the relations between our two countries,” Kim wrote, according to KCNA.
He said strengthening the “comprehensive strategic partnership and alliance” with Russia remained a firm policy of the North Korean government and pledged continued backing for Putin and the Russian Federation.
Kim also said he was convinced that what he called the Russian people’s “sacred war of justice” would end in victory – language Pyongyang has repeatedly used to justify its military support for Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Relations between Moscow and Pyongyang have moved far beyond diplomatic declarations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The two countries signed a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement during Putin’s visit to Pyongyang in June 2024, including a mutual defense clause that significantly expanded military cooperation.
North Korea later deployed thousands of soldiers to Russia, particularly to the Kursk region, where they fought alongside Russian forces.
South Korea’s National Intelligence Service estimated earlier this year that about 6,000 North Korean troops had been killed or wounded in the war. It also estimated that roughly 10,000 North Korean combat troops and another 1,000 engineering personnel were deployed in Russia’s Kursk region.
Separate estimates have put the total number of North Korean soldiers sent to Russia since 2024 at roughly 14,000 to 15,000.
In return, Western and South Korean officials have said Moscow has provided Pyongyang with economic assistance, military technology and battlefield experience.
Kim’s birthday letter also highlighted the increasingly personal nature of his relationship with Putin.
He addressed the Russian leader as his “dearest friend” and closed the message by saying he warmly embraced his “dear comrade,” according to North Korean state media.
The wording reflects a relationship that has grown steadily closer as both governments face international sanctions and political isolation from Western states.
Kim’s latest message made clear that Pyongyang sees that partnership as long-term rather than temporary.

title: Powerful explosions heard in Riyadh
body:

title: Araghchi stresses Coop. with neighbors for regional safety
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 07 (MNA) – Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said continued dialogue and cooperation with neighbours is Iran's chosen path toward building a safer and more stable region.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said continued dialogue and cooperation with neighbours is Iran's chosen path toward building a safer and more stable region, after hosting Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan in Tehran.
In a message on his social media account about hosting his Armenian counterpart, Araghchi said he received Ararat Mirzoyan, Foreign Minister of the Republic of Armenia, in Tehran on Monday, 13 Mehr.
He said the two sides reviewed the expanding relations between Tehran and Yerevan and ways to deepen cooperation in economic, trade, transport, energy and other areas of mutual interest.
Araghchi said they also discussed developments in the Caucasus and the importance of maintaining lasting peace and stability in the region. He said Iran believes regional issues must be resolved with the participation and initiative of regional countries and without interference from extra-regional forces.
The continuation of dialogue and cooperation with neighbours is the path emphasised by the Islamic Republic of Iran to build a safer, more stable and more prosperous region, he said, adding that Iran's neighbours are its priority.

title: Greece takes command of Operation Irini from Italy
body: The Italian Navy has handed command of Operation Irini to the Greek Navy, which will keep the European Union mission in the central Mediterranean and continue enforcing the UN arms embargo on Libya. Greek Navy commander Stavros Polydoros will lead the operation. Three Greek warships — HS Navarinon, Nearchos and Kimon — will take part in the monitoring, backed by two Italian warships. The EU launched Irini on 31 March 2020, after the Berlin Conference on Libya, to enforce the arms embargo set by the UN Security Council. title: Mobile fire teams of BARS-Kursk train to shoot down drones using real UAVs
body:
KURSK, October 7. /TASS/. Mobile fire teams of the BARS-Kursk brigade of Battlegroup North are training to shoot down drones using real UAVs, Company Commander and Senior Training Group Instructor with the call sign Magellan told TASS.
"Our volunteers are training directly, meaning we are killing two birds with one stone: the targets are aerial targets for us, while pilots are also training, with some learning to fly fixed-wing UAVs," the source said, adding that the drones are launched at different angles and from different directions to simulate flights by the Ukrainian army.

title: Houthis say they shot down Saudi drone over Yemen
body:

title: €1,200 Athens Job Splits Greek Reddit on Cost of Living
body: A job offer of €1,100 to €1,200 in Athens is the latest post on r/greece to turn into an argument about whether work in the capital is enough to live on. The writer, posting as Nikosmp88, said they had been offered a role at one of the big gaming companies and asked whether it was worth leaving the provinces. The questions under it were practical: can that salary cover a month, and how do you find a flat if you are already working and cannot sit in Athens house-hunting? One suggestion in the thread was a hotel while you look. The replies treated that as part of the problem, not a solution. A contemporary Greek apartment complex featuring multiple floors and spacious balconies, set amidst lush trees and well-maintained landscaping. The post sits next to a longer one that has been circulating on the same forum: why young people in Greece work and still cannot live. A contributor who left in 2014 argued that the country has built a convenient story about life in Britain, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, and that the harder comparison is at home. They cited Eurostat figures for 2024: Greece had the highest housing-cost overburden rate in the EU, at 28.9 per cent; 19 per cent could not keep the home adequately warm; 43 per cent were behind on mortgage, rent or utility bills. A separate item on the same feed gives the argument a name and a number. The rector of the University of Patras said about 400 students who passed the exams did not enrol this year. Families, he said, are worrying about the rent. None of this is a poll. r/greece is a comment thread, and the salaries in it are offers, not a national average. What the forum is describing is the gap between a job that sounds acceptable and a month that does not close: a gaming salary in Athens, a student place in Patras, and the same question under both.
